Q1 Market Recap: How Private Credit, AI, & War Have Dominated 2026 So Far | The Weekly Wrap

The quarter review links software repricing to private-equity and credit risk, criticizes smoothed private valuations, and separates attractive new lending from legacy exposures. Eisman retains Meritage with a specific year-end buyback expectation and an explicit interest-rate caveat. He expects software incumbents to survive but lose seat and pricing momentum. His universal claim that every 2018-2022 PE software deal is underwater lacks transaction-level support; announced layoffs do not independently establish AI unemployment.

youtube-P1tc75YGjWw-c004 · analytical principle

Widening credit spreads can make new private-credit lending attractive, helping explain large institutional fundraising despite problems in old funds.

Right
Source · 5:55-6:51 ↗
SpeakerSteve Eisman
Stanceconditional
Horizonnot stated
Materialitymajor

The conditional relationship follows from the explicit assumptions; it does not establish that those assumptions hold in observed markets.

Qualification: The particular $10b fundraise totals require original sponsor records; a new fund does not rescue the old one.

Conditional reasoning

Expected net return equals promised income less expected credit losses and costs. A higher spread improves expected return only holding these other terms sufficiently constant.

  • Higher spreads compensate lenders
  • Expected losses, fees and covenants do not worsen enough to offset them

  • Known sector beginning weight
  • Ignoring rebalancing for the simplified calculation

How he reasons here

  • Smooth marks do not erase economic volatility.
  • Separate new lending terms from old-fund recoveries.
  • Use index weights to understand contribution without confusing stock values and GDP.
  • Separate software survival from pricing power.
  • Consider incentives and the timing of credit deterioration.
